content:
Apple must respond by Monday to a complaint filed by Epic Games with the Brazilian antitrust regulator, in which Epic accuses Apple of adopting a restrictive interpretation of its obligations under a recently concluded App Store antitrust agreement in Brazil. Full details below.

A little background

Two months ago, Apple announced that it now allows developers to distribute apps through alternative app marketplaces in Brazil.

This change was part of a settlement that resolved a years-long antitrust investigation, which was triggered by a complaint from Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces and offer payment methods outside of Apple's IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% "Core Technology Fee" on digital goods and services sold through apps distributed outside the App Store. For more on that structure, click here.

Epic questions Apple's execution

According to a report today in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo (via MacMagazine), Epic recently filed a petition with CADE, the Brazilian antitrust regulator, accusing Apple of creating "structural, technical and access-related barriers" that undermine the practical feasibility of alternative app distribution.

Epic noted that, while the new Brazilian terms apply only to iOS apps, Apple's agreement with CADE "expressly covers iPadOS."

Epic is also reportedly objecting to so-called "scare screens" designed to discourage users from installing apps outside the App Store, as well as to the current installation process, which Epic says requires nine steps, compared with Apple's current six-step process in Europe.

According to O Globo, Epic added that Apple's original installation process in Europe required 15 steps, and that after the company was asked to reduce it to six, "download abandonment dropped from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "far exceed what is needed to calculate fees," and said this allows the company "to monitor competitors' business models."

O Globo reported that CADE has given Apple until Monday to submit a response. Apple has not publicly responded to the matter.
